absent: Value of nanoseconds per second and behavior of normalized stamp construction.
Enabled-mode tick dependency tracking, full nohz kick and task switch effects.
Underlying ktime acquisition, offset application, conversion and division helpers.
Clocksource selection, read path and timekeeper locking and update algorithm.
Namespace creation, permission checks, offset freezing rules and host conversion arithmetic.
Timer list layout, queuing, expiry, migration and callback dispatch.

findings.text: Broken-down civil time carries seconds, minutes, hours, month day, month index, years since nineteen hundred, weekday and yearday. Seconds normally span zero to fifty nine with allowance to sixty for a leap second, minutes and hours use conventional clock ranges, month day is one based, month index zero based and weekday Sunday based.

Sixty-four-bit time uses signed seconds plus long nanoseconds. An interval timer specification pairs two such stamps, one for period and one for expiry. Time value aliases distinguish signed and unsigned sixty-four-bit seconds.

Thirty-two-bit compatibility keeps old interval, access-modification and extended control layouts. The interval pairs two old stamps, the buffer holds two old seconds, and the extended control holds mode, frequency and error tuning words plus a timeval stamp and packet and stability counters with trailing padding words.

Per-namespace offsets hold monotonic and boottime adjustments as sixty-four-bit stamps. The namespace object links user namespace, usage counts and common namespace state, stores those offsets, optionally points at a shared version page, and carries a frozen flag that blocks later offset changes after a task joins. A proc offset record pairs a clock identifier with a stamp value. Object layout is randomized.

A cycle counter binds a read callback with a valid-bits mask and fixed-point scale described by multiplier and shift. A time counter adds the counter pointer, last observed cycle, accumulated nanoseconds, conversion mask and fractional remainder, supporting forward accumulation of device cycles into time.

A readable timekeeping base points at a clocksource, records its mask and last cycle, fixed-point scale, nanosecond remainder within the current second, and base values for monotonic and real domains used by lockless readers.

The timekeeper aggregates monotonic and raw readable bases with second counters, wall to monotonic difference, real boot and TAI or auxiliary offsets, coarse remainder and identifier, plus clocksource selection, scale-back parameters, set and change sequence trackers, validity flag, boot or auxiliary difference, cycle and wall intervals, leap trigger, NTP tick error and adjustment state, overflow and skew tracking, and TAI offset.

A system time snapshot captures device and host cycle counts, system and raw monotonic stamps, clocksource identifiers for both, and set and change sequence state with a validity flag. A counter value pairs cycles with identifier and unit choice, and a cross timestamp binds a clock identifier with device time, counter value and system and raw readings.

Signed sixty-four-bit second and ktime extremes use maximum signed value and its negation minus one. Second extremes derive by dividing those extremes by nanoseconds per second. Uptime is bounded at thirty years in seconds, set-time-of-day at second maximum minus uptime bound, and picoseconds per nanosecond is one thousand.

Timer encoding reserves low eighteen bits for CPU selection, one bit for migrating state, and single bits for deferrable, pinned and irqsafe behavior. Combined masks cover base selection, initialization allowance and trace reporting, with array selection shifted by twenty-two and masked in high bits.

Cycle mask helper yields all ones for a given width with saturation at sixty-four bits. Maximum timer lookahead is two to the thirtieth power minus one. CPU prepare and dead handlers for timers are null.
Timekeeper identity enumerates core, optional auxiliary range and count limit. Offset selection enumerates real, boot, TAI and count limit, used to choose which domain offset a ktime query applies.
Each examined time, timer, counter and namespace header defines a private include guard macro that prevents repeated inclusion within one translation unit.

A sixty-four-bit stamp is accepted only with non-negative seconds and nanoseconds below one second. Strict form additionally requires seconds below ktime second maximum to avoid ktime overflow, set-time form requires seconds below set-time maximum to avoid realtime overflow, and an interval specification requires both period and expiry stamps to satisfy the basic check.

Thirty-two-bit time comparison is wrap aware through unsigned subtraction interpreted as signed, giving after and before as inverses. Interval containment compares unsigned distances from the lower bound rather than absolute ordering.

Equality tests both fields, epoch tests both zero, ordering compares seconds then nanoseconds. Addition and subtraction produce normalized stamps, in-place nanosecond addition carries whole seconds, and conversion to scalar nanoseconds clamps at ktime extremes when seconds exceed representable range.

In this configuration hotplug allowance always reports true, tick dependency marking and clearing across global, CPU, task and signal scopes have no effect, full-nohz kick, task switch hook and setup have no effect, and interval timer clearing is empty.
Task switch handling delegates to the internal hook only when full nohz operation is enabled, otherwise it does nothing.

Sixty-four-bit division by thirty-two-bit divisor returns quotient and stores remainder through an out parameter, computed by repeated subtraction while inhibiting compiler transformation into a modulo operation.
Repeated subtraction cost grows with quotient magnitude, so large dividends risk long loops and should not be used where a hardware divider or bounded helper is available.

When namespaces are enabled, monotonic and boottime adjustments add current namespace offsets to a stamp, boot subtraction removes its offset, nanosecond form adds the boot offset in scalar form, and host conversion returns input unchanged for the initial namespace and otherwise delegates with offsets.

When namespaces are disabled, initialization and fork handling are empty, offset helpers are identity, host conversion is identity, commit is empty, version page lookup yields null, namespace get yields null, put is empty, and copy rejects new-time requests while otherwise returning the old namespace.
Enabled namespace handling derives the container from common state, increments references on get and releases with freeing on last put.

Forward conversion scales cycle delta by multiplier, accumulates fractional remainder under caller mask and shifts to nanoseconds. Reverse conversion subtracts stored fraction before shifting. Direct adjustment adds signed delta to accumulated nanoseconds. Timestamp query detects far-future deltas beyond half mask range and treats them as past rather than future.

Treating timestamps beyond half the counter range as old avoids misordering on wrap but misclassifies genuinely stale or far-future readings near the threshold, so callers must sample often relative to counter period.

Timecounter state advances from last cycle through masked delta to accumulated seconds and fraction, with last cycle updated on read and nanosecond total monotonic except for explicit adjustment or backward correction.
Monotonic-derived ktime queries select real, boot or TAI domains through a shared offset mechanism, with raw and coarse counterparts, and monotonic to real translation reuses the same offset path.
Convenience wrappers expose coarse, nanosecond, timespec and seconds forms for boot, TAI, real, raw and monotonic domains, built on the primary offset queries and standard conversions.
Auxiliary clock queries are unavailable in this configuration and report failure without producing a value.

Timer bring-up accepts a timer object, callback and flags, with on-stack variants for scoped objects, and static definition provides a zero-flag preinitialized timer. Initialization variants differ in whether they create a lock class key or pass nulls, with on-stack forms delegating to the keyed helper.
Lock dependency tracking for timers has two build variants, one embedding a static lock class entry keyed by name and one expanding to nothing, selected by configuration.
Pending state reflects hash linkage, container helper recovers the enclosing object from its timer member, stack destruction is a no-op, and isolated-migration exclusion reports zero handled CPUs.
A timer rests detached when idle and becomes linked while queued, with pending observation lockless and initialization required before first queueing.
